Reference & guides

How the pick order works
  1. First: same size, same series, same generation. The closest match: same size, same series, same generation, same platform. Staying at the same size outranks every other change.
  2. Second: same size, same series, next generation. The same series at the same size, one generation newer. Example: a 65QM8K becomes a 65QM8L before any platform change.
  3. Third: same size, same series, different OS. The same series and size on a different platform, last in the main order. The picker keeps the same platform by default. OS swap disclaimer: do not offer a platform change proactively. Offer only if the customer requested that platform, or if the Warranty Team approves it internally. Fire OS is not offered for an OS swap except as an approved exception.
  4. Step-up options are labelled by the jump. Higher series at the same size, same platform, labelled 1st, 2nd, and 3rd upgrade by series levels above the customer’s model. Nothing past the 3rd upgrade is shown. One level at a time is the norm. A 2-level upgrade needs approval first. A 3rd upgrade is shown so the jump is visible, not as a routine pick.
  5. One size step up is separate. A single size up in the same series is not part of the main ranking. It appears on its own below the main picks, clearly marked. It needs the customer’s agreement, noted in the case.
  6. Never a step down on your own. If only a lower tier is available, the customer has to agree first, and the agreement goes in the case notes. If nothing in the order works, escalate to the Warranty Team lead instead of substituting down.
  7. Excluded models drop out. Anything on the Exclude list in step 1 is removed before the order is shown. The first pick on screen is always the first one you have not ruled out.
  8. Blank specs: research first, then a flagged best guess. If a spec needed for a comparison is blank in the source (most often the pack tier or the panel), the picker first checks the library: the same series at another size. If the exact spec is found that way, it is used and marked as filled from the library. If not, the picker uses a best guess, set at the entry level of the model’s display class so a guess never overstates the TV. That suggestion carries an “Estimated spec - validate” flag naming the guessed value. Validate it against the model’s spec sheet or a retailer listing before you offer the TV. Never quote it to the customer as verified. When the customer’s own tier is a guess, step-ups are not ranked off the guess alone. Each candidate is also checked against the customer’s stated specs (backlight class and panel). A candidate below the stated specs is left out as a step down and named as one. The step-ups that remain are flagged as estimated and needing validation, never shown as confirmed upgrades.

Picker notes: where the internal guidance does not line up

Where items conflict, this picker follows the ranking in “How the pick order works” and flags the conflict here rather than picking a side silently. Check the replacement options guide and the Alternate Model Tool before acting on a flagged item.

  • Size step up: a one size step up shows up in the guide’s worked scripts, but not in the guide’s main list of replacement options. So this picker keeps it as a separate, clearly marked option, not a main pick.
  • Platform order: this picker keeps the customer on the same platform by default, yet the guide’s option order still places a different OS third. So different OS picks are shown in the main order but marked, and they need the customer’s agreement.
  • A-stock age limits: the age thresholds for A-stock differ between the main guide and other internal articles. Do not rely on one age cutoff without checking which article applies to the case.
  • 32 inch recertified sets: the current rule for 32 inch recertified replacements differs from what a 2022 article states. Treat the older article as out of date on this point until the guidance is reconciled.
  • Canada: Canada follows a separate recertified only rule, with exceptions. Do not apply the US pick order to a Canadian case without checking the Canadian rule and whether an exception covers it.
  • Bulk OneDrive packs added: 743 pack rows were added to the picker library: Google TV first (327 rows), then Fire TV and Roku TV (416 rows, including 21 Android TV rows labelled as Android TV). 617 of these models are new to the picker and are marked Bulk pack in the list. The other 126 were already in the picker from TCL USA. Nothing about them changed except that their pack source and conflict flag now show on the model.
  • Bulk pack conflicts: 239 of the 743 pack rows carry a conflict flag. A conflict flag means the bulk pack data for that model differed from the existing library value in at least one field. The existing value was kept, and the differing pack value is noted on the model rather than applied. The flag and the pack source are shown on the model itself so the conflict is visible before the model is offered.
  • Blank-spec estimates: 606 of the 743 pack rows state no tier and 317 state no panel. Tier is the column the step-up ranking decides on. Where a blank value is needed for a comparison, the picker fills it from the same series in the library first. Where that series states no value anywhere, it shows a best guess set at the entry level of the model’s display class, marked Estimated on the model and flagged on any suggestion that used it. Treat every Estimated value as unvalidated until it is checked against a spec sheet.
  • Step-up ranking guard: when the customer’s tier is estimated, step-ups are cross-checked against the customer’s stated backlight class and panel before they are shown. A candidate below the stated class is excluded as a step down and named on the model. Example: the 55R646 states Mini LED in its specs but no tier, and its guessed tier 6 once ranked the 55Q651G, a stated QLED, as its 3rd upgrade. The Q651G is now left out as a step down. The step-ups that remain for the R646 are flagged as estimated, not confirmed upgrades.
  • Bulk pack exclusions: models with no verified OS were not added (71 distinct models), and neither were the 2013 PDF models with no smart OS stated. Neither group appears in the packs or in this picker.
About the model data

The pick order follows the internal replacement guide ranking: same size, same series, same generation first, then next generation, then a different OS, with the same platform kept by default and a one size step up kept as a separate option. See the How to Determine Replacement Options guide and the Alternate Model Tool for the full internal guidance. The model list, sizes, and specifications come from TCL USA, checked October 30, 2026: the full tcl.com US store catalog (every TV series, size, and SKU) and the series pages behind it. DisplaySpecifications, retailer MSRP listings, and release-date searches were used as cross-checks only. Where a cross-check disagrees with TCL USA, the page follows TCL USA and the model carries a source check note saying so. List prices are TCL USA list prices or published launch MSRP, never current sale prices, and they only support the ranking. TCL’s designer frame TVs (A300 series) and the FHD Q3 lines are not in the ladder because they are different product types, not step-up or step-down matches for the 4K lines. The picker library also includes the Bulk OneDrive data packs, added October 30, 2026 in this order: the Google TV pack (327 rows) first, then the Fire TV and Roku TV pack (416 rows, including 21 Android TV rows labelled by OS). Pack models carry their size, OS, series, tier, panel, and key specs as stated in the pack, with the pack source and conflict flag shown on the model. Pack data did not overwrite any TCL USA specification already in this picker. Where a pack row conflicts with TCL USA, the TCL USA specification stands and the conflict is flagged in the picker notes and on the model. 71 distinct models with no verified OS and the 2013 PDF models with no smart OS stated were not added.
